axis: FIRST adversarial test of amphora-cro-protocol-packager (zero prior ledger verdicts). Targets the CLAIM-LOCK path (claim_locks map, all 8 REQUIRED_CRO_CLAIM_LOCKS) and the execution_authority_locked path (execution_authorized scalar, ranking_eligible, authority_ceiling) of the live CroProtocolPackageV2 signed-packet contract, plus the previously-unexamined locked_numeric_thresholds / protocol_lock_sha256 binding pair.
claim_under_attack: amphora-cro-protocol-packager/docs/mission.md (campaign item T-02 claim_text): amphora-cro-protocol-packager has never received an adversarial verdict; its constructive SIGNED_RECEIPT-era receipts (8/8 CRO claim-locks true + sign-verify round-trip 1.0 at n=5, cro-protocol-packager-signed-packet-kpi.v1.json) are untested claims about the strength of the packager's claim-lock and execution-authority enforcement.
does_not_close: No live production or CLI code path was found that reads locked_numeric_thresholds or protocol_lock_sha256 for any purpose (grepped whole workspace: these two fields appear ONLY inside CroProtocolPackageV2's own definition and its format-only validate() arm). This receipt does not show a packet-authored threshold being used to make a live pass/fail decision anywhere today -- it shows that the signed-packet contract's OWN claim-lock machinery accepts and signs one, which is what the pre-committed refutation_criterion names ('a packet-authored threshold is accepted'), independent of whether a consumer exists yet.

If any future code path is added that reads locked_numeric_thresholds as an authoritative decision input (e.g. a CRO acceptance gate), trusting protocol_lock_sha256 as proof the thresholds were host-set rather than packet-authored, it would be trivially forgeable exactly as demonstrated here -- this is the live risk this finding flags for repair, not a hypothetical.

The 8-alternate-encoding sub-harness (V1-V8 x 2 paths) found 0 leaks; taken alone it would license CLAIM_SURVIVED for the claim-lock and execution-authority-locked deserialization boundary specifically. The module-level verdict is REFUTED because of the separate (d) threshold-binding finding, not because the encoding harness found a leak.

This probe exercises the Rust runtime only (CroProtocolPackageV2 in amphora-assurance-capabilities). It does not probe amphora-cli's invocation surface or any HTTP/CLI boundary that might construct a packet from untrusted input before calling these APIs.

headline: REFUTED: directive attack (d) -- a packet-authored performance/decision threshold in locked_numeric_thresholds, paired with a format-valid but content-undereived protocol_lock_sha256 ("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa...", never the hash of anything), was ACCEPTED end-to-end: validate()=Ok, sign()=Ok, verify_signature()=Ok (validate_ok=True, sign_ok=True, verify_signature_ok=True). protocol_lock_sha256 is format-checked (64 lowercase hex) but never content-bound to locked_numeric_thresholds anywhere in the codebase -- no producer or consumer computes it as a hash of the thresholds it claims to lock. A positive control (same construction with protocol_lock_sha256 omitted) IS correctly rejected (positive_control_missing_lock_hash_rejected=True), proving the harness discriminates a real binding defect rather than being vacuously green. Separately: directive probes (a) execution_authorized->true, (b) strip/null each of the 8 REQUIRED_CRO_CLAIM_LOCKS in turn (16 probes), and (c) a one-byte flip inside the DSSE-signed payload of an already-signed packet, ALL fail closed (17 additional probes beyond (d), 0 slipped through). The 8-alternate-encoding injection harness (V1-V8, same taxonomy as the amphora-candidate-contract T-01 probe) run against both the claim-lock path and the execution_authority_locked path (16 vector/path combinations) found 0 leaks -- all 16 EVADED, because execution_authorized is a strict top-level scalar field behind #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] (any misnamed/wrapped encoding fails at deserialize) and claim_locks required-key membership is checked exactly by string equality (any misnamed/homoglyph key fails the required-lock presence check at validate()). The encoding harness alone would have licensed CLAIM_SURVIVED; the directive (d) threshold-binding finding overrides that to CLAIM_REFUTED for the module as a whole, because refutation_criterion item (iii) ("a packet-authored threshold is accepted") DID occur.
non_circularity: Uses the REAL compiled amphora-assurance-capabilities crate's CroProtocolPackageV2::draft/validate/sign/verify_signature (same public API amphora-cli and the module's own Phase-0 KPI harness use), invoked from a Rust #[test] integration test in the crate's own tests/ directory (amphora-assurance-capabilities/tests/cro_protocol_packager_t02_adversarial_probe.rs), compiled and run via `cargo test -p amphora-assurance-capabilities --offline`. Not a Python re-implementation of validate()/sign()/verify_signature().
refutation_criterion_statement: REFUTATION DID OCCUR via directive attack (d): a packet-authored performance/decision threshold (locked_numeric_thresholds) WAS accepted through validate()/sign()/verify_signature() when paired with a format-valid but content-undereived protocol_lock_sha256. This is exactly clause (iii) of the refutation_criterion ("a packet-authored threshold is accepted"). Clauses (i) ("any mutation verifies") and (ii) ("any lock is bypassable") did NOT occur in the remaining 34 probes (19 directive-(a)/(b)/(c) probes minus the (d) group, plus 16 encoding x path combinations): execution_authorized=true, all 16 strip/null claim-lock mutations, and the one-byte signed-payload flip all failed closed, and all 16 alternate-encoding vector/path combinations were evaded.
refutation_criterion_verbatim: Any mutation verifies, any lock is bypassable, or a packet-authored threshold is accepted.
theory_reference: Saltzer & Schroeder (1975) 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems' Proceedings of the IEEE 63(9):1278-1308 -- complete mediation requires every field that participates in a trust decision to be independently authenticated, not merely format-checked; a field that LOOKS like a cryptographic binding (a 64-hex-char 'lock' hash) but is never computed from the content it claims to bind provides no actual integrity guarantee. NIST FIPS 180-4 (2015) SHA-256 -- a hash is only a binding if the verifier recomputes and compares it against the bound content; format validity (length + alphabet) is not content validity. in-toto Attestation v1.0 (2020) / DSSE -- the signed envelope faithfully protects EXACTLY the bytes it signs (this receipt's directive-(c) one-byte-flip probe confirms that layer holds); it cannot protect against a field inside those bytes that was never bound to anything in the first place.
